name: TCCC Digital Casualty Card
title: Documenting care when every handoff matters.
role: Product design · UX research · Interaction design · Prototyping
summary: A mobile-first concept for documenting casualty information and supporting continuity of information during medical handoffs. Informed by conversations with combat medics and desk research into US and NATO field documentation.
status: Interactive UX prototype · Not clinically validated

sections.title: 01 / Context & challenge
body: Casualty documentation moves between people, environments and stages of care. The design challenge was to reduce documentation friction without making uncertain information appear complete or verified.
This is a conceptual interface rather than an approved clinical system. The portfolio case separates original research activities from later reconstruction and design hypotheses.

sections.title: 02 / Discover — Primary research
body: I spoke with combat medics to understand documentation practices and the constraints of recording information during field care. Original interview transcripts, participant counts and direct quotes are not included in the available project materials; this case therefore does not attribute specific findings or numerical results to participants.

Research artifact: a structured interview guide covering context of use, information priorities, interruptions, unidentified casualties, handoffs, connectivity, correction of mistakes and privacy. Questions focused on actual workflows rather than hypothetical feature preferences.

Research synthesis (design hypotheses, not verified interview statistics): allow unknown values, preserve draft state, distinguish documentation from transmission, and prevent loss of work when a user changes sections.

sections.title: 03 / Discover — Desk research & benchmark
body: I examined the documentation model around the US TCCC Casualty Card (DD Form 1380), including the MIST sequence: Mechanism of injury, Injuries, Signs and symptoms, Treatments. NATO-related field medical documentation was part of the comparative research scope, but this prototype is not represented as STANAG-certified.

Competitive artifact: a feature comparison between paper documentation, conventional long forms and a digital structured flow. Criteria: speed of entry, traceability, visibility of unknown information, handoff clarity, offline behavior, and accessibility.
Reference resources: Joint Trauma System and the official DD Form 1380. These materials inform the information architecture; they are not evidence of official endorsement or medical validation.

sections.title: 04 / Define — Problem framing
body: How might we support a combat medic in recording and handing over accurate casualty information under interruptions, limited time and uncertain connectivity, while clearly communicating incomplete or unverified fields?
Jobs to be done: capture the information available now; return to an unfinished record; review before handing off; understand what has and has not been saved or transferred.

Prioritization artifact: P0 — reliable draft persistence, straightforward navigation, meaningful errors and incomplete/unknown states. P1 — structured handoff review and export. Later — authenticated device-to-device exchange, encryption, audit log and medically validated terminology.

sections.title: 05 / Develop — Information architecture & user flow
body: The redesigned prototype is organized as Identify → Mechanism → Injuries → Signs → Treatments → Review. Each section is directly reachable; users can move backward or save a partial record.

Alternative path artifact: unidentified casualty → create a temporary record → enter available MIST information → keep draft → add identification later. Other branches cover interrupted entry, missing details, invalid persistence and export without confirmed receipt.

Information model: unique record ID, identification, mechanism, injuries, observations, interventions, documentation author, time and record status. Real clinical deployment would need stricter field definitions, secure timestamps, structured events and authorized review.

sections.title: 06 / Develop — Interaction and UI decisions
body: The interface uses a restrained, high-contrast visual hierarchy, clear step position, large touch targets, consistent input labels, explicit actions and concise status messages.
The core distinction is between Saved locally, Reviewed and Exported. No sharing action is allowed to imply successful receipt by another person without confirmation.
Content decisions: unknown values should not be silently replaced with arbitrary defaults; editing an existing record must open that record rather than a new empty one.

sections.title: 07 / Deliver — Code-based audit & remediation
body: A code review of the earlier React prototype identified simulated saving, disconnected mock listings, false-positive transmission indicators, simulated voice recognition and sections that could be bypassed without coordinated validation.

The revised demonstration replaces the primary experience with a coherent MIST flow, local browser draft storage, editable saved records, clear persistence errors, final review and a downloadable JSON demonstration export.
These are implementation changes supported by source review, not results from a completed field usability study. Browser-based end-to-end QA and clinical/security validation remain necessary.

sections.title: 08 / Evaluation plan & limitations
body: Proposed usability tasks: create an unidentified casualty draft; interrupt and resume; change previously entered information; review missing documentation; export a record; recover from a failed local save. Measure task completion, critical errors, recovery success and understanding of transmission status.
Recommended test environments: small mobile viewport, keyboard-only use, screen reader, network interruption, storage failure and realistic time constraints with de-identified scenarios.

This prototype is not intended for real patient data or medical decision-making. Production requirements include authenticated access, encrypted storage and transmission, audit trails, medical subject-matter validation, retention rules and secure offline synchronization.

name: Affinity Agreements Engine
title: Making complex agreements easier to manage.
role: Product UX/UI · Enterprise workflows · Data-heavy UI
summary: An internal enterprise platform connecting vehicle records, offers, organisations and vouchers. Redesigned navigation recovers 168 px of workspace.

sections.title: The challenge
body: Affinity Agreements Engine connects vehicle inventories, commercial offers, organisations, members and vouchers through administrative workflows. The challenge was to reduce cognitive load without losing the business rules essential to operational work.
My scope covered navigation patterns, data-heavy tables, interaction states, and consistent access to connected workflows.

sections.title: Discover — audit and system mapping
body: I reviewed existing interface requirements and flows across Vehicle Library, Create Vehicle, Vehicle Details, Offers, Organisations and Vouchers. I identified constraints in horizontal workspace, interaction consistency and navigation clarity.

Entity analysis established key dependencies: vehicle records can be reused across offers; Shared and Bespoke offers behave differently; published offers have restricted actions; organisations and members have their own relationships.

sections.title: Define — from entities to workflows
body: The core problem statement was: How might we simplify complex administrative workflows while preserving accurate information, clear relationships and predictable business rules?

I organised the To-Be experience around connected list views, detail screens, creation flows, relevant states and contextual actions. The key UX decision was to model business objects before refining visual presentation.

sections.title: Develop — navigation redesign
body: I designed an expanded sidebar and a 72 px compact navigation rail, returning 168 px of horizontal space to dense tables. The compact mode includes accessible navigation names and user-persisted preference.
The interface also considered overlay expansion, keyboard dismissal and predictable behaviour when moving between modules.

sections.title: Develop — offer workflows and tables
body: I structured Create a Shared Offer and Apply an Existing Shared Offer as distinct journeys with clear entry points and review steps. The flows separate reusable offer configuration from assignment.
The Vehicle Library and connected modules prioritise scannable tables, consistent actions, relevant detail information and clear handling of incomplete, restricted or unavailable records.

sections.title: Design system and interaction states
body: Reusable navigation, table, detail and form patterns bring consistency across modules. I accounted for empty states, unsaved changes, validation feedback and state-specific actions, so that the same interaction principles work beyond a single screen.

sections.title: Legacy CRM migration — extension scenario
body: As a complementary product-strategy exercise, I mapped how this architecture could support a transition away from a legacy CRM. The method covers an As-Is inventory, To-Be data model, source-to-target mapping, record reconciliation, RBAC permissions, and integration states.

The proposed phased rollout includes controlled pilots, parallel verification, cutover planning and post-launch monitoring. This extension illustrates my approach to enterprise modernisation; it is not a claim that I performed a production migration for Affinity.

sections.title: Outcomes and live prototype
body: The navigation redesign recovers 168 px of working width for data-heavy tables. Clearer separation of offer creation and assignment supports a more coherent workflow and reusable interaction architecture.
Explore the interactive prototype using the Original project archive link below. It demonstrates Offers, Vehicles, Organisations and Vouchers navigation and representative administrative flows.

name: Semaverse
title: Intelligence, made legible.
summary: Making AI work understandable: connected research, visible progress, and document changes people can review and recover.

sections.title: The challenge
body: Investment work depends on complex documents, structured financial data, and a reliable record of changes. Adding AI makes the interface responsible for explaining both the information and the system’s actions.

At Semaverse, I led the end-to-end redesign and rollout of core product workflows. My focus was making document handling, financial data, and AI interactions predictable enough to support confident decisions.

sections.title: My contribution
body: As the solo product designer, I worked across research, interaction design, interface design, and implementation with engineers. My scope included document upload, saving, versioning, management, data tables, forms, and AI-agent interactions.
I conducted user research and usability testing, then worked with engineering to make the proposed behavior feasible and resilient to edge cases.

sections.title: Make the document lifecycle explicit
body: I redesigned the upload, save, version, and document-management flows as connected parts of one experience. Clear progression mattered because people needed to know where a document stood before relying on it.

I defined distinct viewing, editing, processing, and saved states. These states made the difference between a user action and a completed system action visible, supporting transparency and auditability.

sections.title: Give AI actions a readable context
body: I designed interactions with agents that analyze, interpret, and help people navigate documents. The interaction work focused on making AI actions and the current system state understandable.
The same principle carried into structured financial data: predictable flows, legible tables, and clear forms helped users move between source material and analysis.

sections.title: Design for the whole system
body: Reusable interaction rules and patterns connected the individual workflows. This gave engineering a consistent basis for implementation rather than a collection of unrelated screens.
Collaboration continued through technical constraints and edge cases, where a visually complete screen still needed precise behavior.

sections.title: What changed
body: The work improved the usability and reliability of core workflows, reduced confusion around AI actions and system states, and strengthened traceability. These are qualitative outcomes documented in my CV; no numerical performance claims are attached to this project.

caption: Current public Semaverse product image. Shown for product context; it may include changes made after my engagement ended in January 2026.

name: Lumio · Couples spending
title: Shared money, without shared-everything pressure.
summary: I made shared spending the first useful experience: partners could understand joint costs while choosing which transactions stayed private. In a separate 30-day onboarding experiment, reported partner invitations rose from 19% to 44% and bank connections from 55% to 71%.

sections.title: At a glance
body: Product: Lumio, a personal-finance product for couples. Problem: help partners understand shared costs across separate accounts without requiring them to expose every purchase.

My role: sole designer on couples spending, from research and product definition through interface design, testing, and delivery. Team: I worked with product and engineering; activation decisions were shaped with the CEO and COO. Timeline: from 2022; the source does not specify an end date.

Related activation evidence: a separate reported 30-day onboarding experiment moved partner invitations from 19% to 44% and bank connections from 55% to 71%. These are experiment outcomes, not measured impact attributable to the couples-spending release.

sections.title: The challenge
body: Couples managing money across separate bank accounts needed a way to see shared expenses and recurring commitments together. The product was moving beyond automatic savings, so the team had to choose a useful first experience without assuming couples wanted fully joint finances.

The constraints were a small team, backend and frontend effort, and sensitive financial information. The experience needed to make shared costs legible while giving each person control over what they disclosed.

sections.title: My ownership
body: I owned the couples-spending design from discovery through delivery: I reviewed research, facilitated product-definition workshops, mapped the experience, designed the shared-spending views and transaction controls, prototyped interactions, and prepared handoff and test cases.

I made the design recommendations and delivered more than 200 screens and 14 microprototypes. Product and engineering partners helped prioritize feasibility and worked through test cases before launch. The separate onboarding experiment was cross-functional work with the CEO and COO; I do not claim its results as an outcome of the spending release.

sections.title: Key decisions
body: Start with shared spending. We completed 32 of 35 planned interviews; the research highlighted a practical need to understand money across different accounts and track shared expenses. I recommended shared spending as the first release because it answered that need and fit the small team’s delivery capacity. Seven macro jobs to be done and a value-versus-effort workshop helped align the wider opportunity with a shippable scope.

Show the shared picture, preserve personal control. Couples needed to understand contributions and recurring costs, but not every transaction was necessarily joint. I designed a shared breakdown with partner contributions, upcoming payments, and transaction-level controls to share or hide purchases. This made the shared view useful without treating account visibility as all-or-nothing.

Make financial context scannable. A breakdown, collaborator cards, and labels for accounts and payments show how spending relates to each partner and shared commitments. The design surfaced recurring costs and upcoming payments alongside the overview so users could interpret totals in context.

sections.title: Result
body: The couples-spending experience was delivered, supported by more than 200 screens, 14+ microprototypes, and design-system updates. The source does not provide feature-level activation, adoption, or retention measurements, so I cannot quantify the release’s direct impact.

Separately, the onboarding case reports a 30-day experiment: partner invitations increased from 19% to 44% (+25 percentage points), and bank connections from 55% to 71% (+16 points). The source omits sample sizes, complete control data, and statistical significance; treat these as reported results, not proven long-term lift or causal impact from this case.

sections.title: Reflection
body: With more time, I would connect the shared-spending release to a defined activation funnel and track whether partners reach a first shared moment, return to review costs, and keep sharing preferences enabled.

For the reported onboarding experiment, I would want sample sizes, the full control-versus-variant results, and a significance read before drawing a firm conclusion. That evidence would help distinguish a promising short-term change from a durable improvement.

caption: Lumio’s public product presentation of shared spending and recurring expenses.

name: Lumio · Activation
title: Get couples to their first shared moment.
summary: I used funnel analysis to identify two points of friction, then helped shape a smaller onboarding experiment. In the reported 30-day test, partner invitations rose from 19% to 44% and bank connections from 55% to 71%.

sections.title: At a glance
body: Product: Lumio, a personal-finance app for couples. Problem: too few people moved from registration to becoming an activated couple and experiencing shared value.

My role: Senior Product Designer, defining the activation moment, mapping the journey, designing and prototyping onboarding options, and preparing test cases. Team: I worked with the CEO, COO, product and engineering. Timeline: a reported 30-day experiment; the source does not specify the full project dates.

Outcome: partner invitations increased from 19% to 44% (+25 percentage points); bank connections increased from 55% to 71% (+16 points). The source does not provide sample sizes, complete control data, or statistical significance.

sections.title: The challenge
body: The product needed more couples to reach a first shared moment, not simply more completed registrations. Funnel analysis in Mixpanel showed a drop-off around creating a Shared Space. Bank connection created a separate hesitation: users wanted reassurance about security, a clear reason to connect, and a way to explore before committing.
The design had to reduce unnecessary setup without obscuring why a bank connection mattered. Product and engineering capacity also shaped what could be tested first.

sections.title: My ownership
body: I worked with the CEO and COO to define activation, mapped the journey backward from that outcome, and translated the funnel evidence into design hypotheses. I developed four onboarding flow options, shortlisted two, built prototypes, incorporated internal test feedback, and prepared TestFlight test cases.

Product and engineering partners helped assess feasibility and sequence the work. The reported result belongs to the cross-functional experiment; the source does not isolate my design contribution from other changes.

sections.title: Key decisions
body: Automate Shared Space creation. The Mixpanel funnel showed a substantial drop-off at this setup step. I proposed removing the configuration task so couples could reach the shared experience sooner. This traded early user control over setup for a shorter path to value; the design direction explored creating the space automatically.

Explain and reassure before bank connection. Research and funnel context pointed to security questions and unclear value as barriers. I explored clearer reassurance and a stronger explanation of why connecting an account helps, while letting people explore before committing.

Narrow four flow options to two. Competitor review and internal prototype testing helped compare alternatives. I kept the shortlist focused so backend work could start alongside UI development, then used another iteration and TestFlight test cases to prepare the experiment.

sections.title: Result
body: The reported 30-day A/B test showed partner invitations moving from 19% to 44% (+25 percentage points) and bank connections from 55% to 71% (+16 points). These are reported experiment results; without sample sizes, complete control data, or statistical significance, they should be treated as directional evidence rather than proven durable lift.
The test focused on two meaningful steps toward shared value, rather than registration alone. The available source does not include longer-term activation, retention, or downstream couple engagement.

sections.title: Reflection
body: With more time, I would validate the automatic Shared Space hypothesis with users who want to configure their finances themselves, and make the choice easy to revisit after onboarding.

I would also secure the full experiment readout before interpreting the lift: sample sizes, control and variant counts, confidence, and follow-up behavior. That would show whether the improved first steps translated into sustained use by both partners.

name: Oasive
title: Making specialist finance feel clear.
summary: A website for an AI fixed-income platform, connecting a complex product story with a clear visual hierarchy, interactive demonstrations, and considered motion.
caption: The final Oasive website’s public preview, retrieved from oasive.ai. Product content may evolve after handoff.

sections.title: The challenge
body: Oasive brings research, screening, analysis, valuation, and reporting into one workflow for fixed-income professionals. The website needed to make that breadth understandable while retaining the credibility and precision expected in institutional finance.
My task was to translate a specialist product into a clear website experience: explain what it does, show how the workflow connects, and help visitors understand the available levels of access.

sections.title: My contribution
body: I designed the website in Figma and directed its translation into a responsive implementation. My work covered the page structure, visual hierarchy, reusable interface patterns, product presentation, and the refinement of motion and responsive behavior.

I continued iterating after the initial handoff, revisiting the layout, animations, and adaptations that I felt needed more attention. That additional work brought the execution closer to the quality I wanted for the product.

sections.title: Explain a connected workflow
body: The page moves from a concise product promise into the five stages of the fixed-income workflow: Research, Screen, Analyze, Value, and Report. Each stage has a specific job, rather than appearing as another disconnected feature.

The workflow ends with an investment decision and a feedback loop into the next research question. This makes the relationship between the stages visible and gives the product demonstrations that follow a useful context.

sections.title: Balance editorial clarity with technical detail
body: The visual language pairs serif headlines with compact, monospaced labels and a restrained navy-and-teal palette. The large type establishes the message; smaller labels organize the technical content without making every element compete for attention.

I used the Figma styles, tokens, and component families as a consistent foundation for buttons, tabs, cards, plans, and navigation. During refinement, I adjusted spacing, section rhythm, borders, and the framing of the product visuals.

sections.title: Let the product explain itself
body: The demo section organizes the platform into four entry points: research reports, Ask Oasive, the MBS dashboard, and valuation with scenario analysis. Short explanations sit alongside product demonstrations so visitors can connect a capability to something they can see.

The animated hero introduces the relationship between the workspace, research desk, and supporting evidence. I refined the presentation and motion around these materials as part of the website experience.

sections.title: Make the levels of access legible
body: The pricing section distinguishes free research, macro research with chat, and the specialist agency MBS platform. Its hierarchy gives each plan a clear identity and separates the main offer, included capabilities, limitations, and next action.
Research articles and the founder section add context around the product. Their layouts needed enough space for substantive information while remaining consistent with the rest of the page.

sections.title: Carry the detail across screen sizes
body: I revisited the desktop, tablet, and mobile layouts, including the product-demo tabs, text wrapping, and the proportions of the founder image. The aim was to preserve the reading order and the usefulness of each section as the available space changed.

Motion was refined alongside the layout, with reduced-motion support retained in the implementation. I treated animation as part of how the website explains the product, with readability and responsive behavior carrying equal weight.

sections.title: The final result
body: The website is live at oasive.ai, bringing the product story, workflow, demonstrations, access plans, and company information into a coherent experience.

The delivered work brings together the Figma design foundation, a responsive website, product demonstrations, and motion refinements. My contribution connects product understanding with the practical details of bringing a website to completion.

name: Welltrax
title: Clarity, for the long haul.
summary: A tablet-first logistics experience for drivers managing pickups, deliveries, and shifting conditions in the field.

sections.title: The working environment
body: Drivers manage time-sensitive pickups and deliveries in remote locations, with intermittent connectivity and frequent changes. The redesign had to account for these conditions, as well as the information needed for operations and billing.

sections.title: Scope and constraints
body: The initial release targeted iPads, with Android and possible smartphone adaptation in mind. I used the company’s branding as a foundation while moving beyond the legacy app’s visual approach.
The source case is marked NDA. This page summarizes the shared project description; detailed screens and a walkthrough are available by request.

sections.title: Make the next action clear
body: The core workflows covered arrival, load management, and departure. Drivers could confirm or decline a new pickup and review a load before or during a trip.
Contact management accounted for information learned in the field: adding, editing, and removing a person with multiple phone numbers directly from pickup or drop details.

sections.title: Handle operational detail
body: Tank sections supported multiple tanks and different gauging methods. Horizontally scrolling tabs and overflow menus accommodated that complexity without crowding the main task.
Duration tracking captured arrival, loading, and waiting times. Photo and video attachments supported receipts and other documentation. Field-level validation and general errors guided correction.

sections.title: Account for shared devices and night work
body: Two or three regular drivers could use the same device, and a driver might work with different trucks or transporters. The sign-in and shift flows needed to accommodate those changes, including signing out after choosing the wrong transporter.
Night mode responded to night driving, while an offline-first approach reflected unreliable connectivity. These were core working conditions, not optional aesthetic preferences.

sections.title: Iteration and delivery
body: Stakeholder feedback, including drivers and internal teams, informed the prototypes. Testing with representative users helped refine usability. The work also included a UI kit; the shared source does not report quantified post-launch results.

body: I reviewed the existing platform structure and brand guidelines, then clarified user requirements with the client. The structure covered the main page, course page, and section page.

sections.title: Support course discovery
body: Course descriptions, audience information, partner logos, and contact details formed the key content. Low-fidelity wireframes established the layout before moving to high-fidelity prototypes.

sections.title: Refine and hand over
body: Client feedback informed iterations in layout, color, and typography. I delivered the three page designs and their UI elements in Figma. The source does not provide measured learning or registration outcomes.

name: El Ticko
title: From finding a service to taking the next step.
summary: Designing a website that helps New York residents understand and contact a tick-extermination service.

sections.title: The challenge
body: People needed accessible information about service areas, qualifications, pricing, and booking. The design brief brought those needs into a clearer service website.

sections.title: Research and structure
body: The original case records approximately 67 survey responses and competitor research. Difficulty finding service information informed the task flows and information architecture.

sections.title: Develop the design
body: I worked through a moodboard, concept agreement, and final design. The page set included Home, About Us, Tick Spraying, Contact Us, and Service Area, supported by a UI kit.

sections.title: Outcome and target
body: The delivered work was the website design. The source names a 30% increase in customers as a launch goal; it is a target, not an achieved result.

name: Projector Institute
title: Helping designers build their own judgment.
summary: Guiding students from a problem they care about to a complete mobile-app concept.

sections.title: The learning challenge
body: Students approached their coursework as if they were building a startup: choose a meaningful problem, investigate it, and develop a mobile-app solution. They could select their own topic or work from a suggested list.

sections.title: My role
body: I guided the process as mentor and curator, supporting research, ideation, prototyping, testing, and iteration. The app concepts and designs belong to the students; my contribution is teaching and feedback.

sections.title: Connect foundations to practice
body: The course covered iOS guidelines, Material Design, user flows, navigation, forms, typography, and visual hierarchy. Students applied these foundations within their own product concepts.

Later work included interaction patterns, prototyping, testing, animation, and an introduction to marketing. Research and user feedback helped students refine their proposals rather than stop at the first visual direction.

sections.title: The outcome
body: Students produced full mobile-app design projects and gained experience carrying an idea through a structured process. The original showcase contains their coursework and is credited as student work.

name: Moderated usability research
title: Test the first experience, before explaining it.
summary: A work-in-progress plan for comparing sign-up, setup, and empty-space experiences.

sections.title: The study plan
body: The source outlines live, moderated testing during delivery. Three comparisons were planned: Sign-up A versus B, Setup A versus B, and Empty Space A versus B.

sections.title: Recruit for a relevant first encounter
body: The plan calls for five to eight respondents from the target audience. Participants should not be the team, friends, or family, and should not have seen the setup or received the product link in advance.

sections.title: Work in progress
body: This is a research plan, not a completed study. The shared material does not contain sessions, findings, or outcomes, so no results are presented.
